scenario: Writer publishes results of an in-house customer survey and states the survey mode, the target population, how respondents were recruited from an opt-in panel, and the exact question wording used.
Writer cites a headline statistic from a third-party survey but never states how the sample was collected, what population it represents, or the exact question that produced the number.
Writer presents results from a self-selected opt-in web panel using the same confident 'nationally representative, +/-2%' language normally reserved for a probability-based sample.
Writer reports that '68% of respondents preferred Option A' in a pull quote with no sample size given anywhere in the post, including in a footnote.
Writer reports a subgroup finding ('72% of remote workers under 25 agreed') without stating how many respondents were in that subgroup.
Writer reports the topline statistic alongside its sample size and the margin of sampling error for the probability-based panel that produced it.
Writer ran the same dataset through a dozen different subgroup cuts, found one significant result, and published only that cut without mentioning the other eleven tests.
Writer discloses in the methodology section that fourteen comparisons were run on the dataset and explains which correction was applied before highlighting the significant result.
Writer had a thesis in mind before analysis, found the full dataset didn't support it, and quietly published only the two data points that did fit the narrative.
Headline reads 'Remote Work Causes Higher Burnout' based on a purely observational correlational survey with no controlled or randomized design behind it.

Writer reports 'companies that adopted the tool saw higher retention' from observational data and explicitly labels it a correlation, noting other explanations are possible, since no randomized study was run.
A chart's y-axis is truncated to start at 80 instead of 0, making a 3-point difference between two bars look like a threefold difference.
Writer builds a bar chart with a zero-based axis and proportions that visually match the actual size of the underlying difference reported in the text.
Before publishing, the writer confirms sample size, margin of error, survey mode, and exact question wording are all disclosed, and reviews every chart's axis for distortion.
Writer ships the post with a chart whose visual bar heights suggest a much larger gap than the substantiated numbers in the prose actually show, and no one reviewed the chart before publishing.
